body:
Charge for house cleaning by time, then check the price by square foot. In 2026, HomeGuide puts hourly rates at $25 to $75 per hour per cleaner, standard cleaning at $0.10 to $0.17 per square foot, and a typical standard visit in the $120 to $280 range. If both methods land near the same number, your quote is sound. If they do not, your time estimate is off.

## 2026 market rates to price against

Use the market as a fence, not a target. Your price has to cover your labor, supplies, travel, insurance, and taxes first, then sit inside what customers in your area already pay.

| Pricing method | Standard clean | Deep clean |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Per hour, per cleaner | $25 to $75 | $25 to $75, more hours |
| Per square foot | $0.10 to $0.17 | $0.11 to $0.30 |
| Per visit, typical home | $120 to $280 | $230 to $600 |

HomeGuide 2026 data gives those ranges. The same source lists move out cleaning at $0.22 to $0.33 per square foot, the highest of the three, because empty homes need inside cabinets, inside appliances, and every surface done at once.

Angi 2026 data is close. Angi puts a standard visit at $118 to $238 with an average of $176, and deep cleaning at $180 to $375 with an average of $260, at $25 to $70 per hour. Two sources, same ballpark. Price below both ranges and you will be busy and underpaid. Price above them and you need reviews and a clear reason, like pet heavy homes or post construction work.

Clean type drives the gap. A standard clean covers kitchens, bathrooms, floors, dusting, and trash. A deep clean adds baseboards, inside appliances, tracks, and grout. Price the first visit as a deep clean. The home has build up your recurring price was never built to cover.

## The pricing formula: time first, square foot check second

**Price = Estimated hours x Your hourly rate**

**Check price = Home square feet x Rate per square foot for the clean type**

Pick your hourly rate from your costs, not from a rival ad. Add up what an hour on site really costs you: pay, payroll tax if you have help, supplies, fuel, insurance, and a margin for profit. Many solo cleaners need $40 to $55 per hour billed to clear a fair wage after costs. A company with employees, bonding, and insurance often needs $50 to $75.

Then estimate time by walking the home, in person or by video. Count bathrooms twice in your head. A bathroom takes longer than a bedroom of the same size, every time. Note pets, clutter, and how long since the last pro clean. Write the estimate down. After the job, compare real time to estimated time and fix your notes for that home. Three visits in, your times will be close.

If you price other home services too, the same habit works there. See our [handyman pricing calculator](/blog/handyman-pricing-calculator/) for small jobs, and lay quotes out with our [free estimate template](/blog/free-estimate-template/). Check profit on each job with the [markup vs margin calculator](/blog/markup-vs-margin-calculator/).

## Worked example: a 2,000 sq ft home, standard and recurring

Say a client has a 2,000 sq ft (186 sq m) home, 3 bedrooms and 2 bathrooms, in average shape, with one dog. They want a first standard clean, then every two weeks.

Step 1, time estimate. Kitchen 45 minutes, 2 bathrooms at 30 minutes each is 60 minutes, bedrooms and living areas 75 minutes, floors throughout 60 minutes. Total: 45 + 60 + 75 + 60 = 240 minutes, or 4 hours for one cleaner.

Step 2, time price. Your rate is $50 per hour. 4 hours x $50 = $200 for the first standard clean.

Step 3, square foot check. 2,000 sq ft x $0.10 per sq ft = $200. The two methods agree at $200, inside the HomeGuide standard range for a 2,000 sq ft home of $190 to $340 for regular cleaning. Quote $200.

Step 4, recurring price. A home cleaned every two weeks takes less time, say 3 hours once the build up is gone. 3 x $50 = $150 per visit. As a discount check, $200 x 0.85 with a 15 percent recurring discount = $170. The time method gives the sharper, honest price here, so quote $150 to $170 and pick one figure to put in writing. This example uses $160, the middle, stated as a flat per visit price.

Step 5, first visit as a deep clean. If the home has not been pro cleaned in six months, price visit one as deep. At $0.18 per sq ft, inside the $0.11 to $0.30 deep range: 2,000 x $0.18 = $360. Time check: about 7 hours x $50 = $350. Close enough. Quote $360, rounded up, and say in writing that later visits drop to the recurring price.

Check step 5 again: $360 / 2,000 = $0.18 per sq ft, and $360 / $50 = 7.2 hours of paid time. If your crew of two finishes in 3.5 hours on site, that is 7 labor hours. The math holds both ways.

## Quote checklist you can use today

Take this list on every walkthrough.

- Home size in square feet, bedrooms, and bathrooms
- Clean type: standard, deep, or move out
- Time since last pro clean, and problem areas named by the client
- Pets, shedding, and litter areas
- Add-ons priced apart: inside fridge $12 to $50, inside oven $15 to $35, interior windows $4 to $7 each, laundry $5 to $20 per load (HomeGuide add-on ranges)
- Supplies: who provides them, and any product the client bans
- Travel time and parking, built into the price, not added later
- Recurring schedule offered at the quote, with the lower repeat price in writing

Add-ons are where small firms leave money on the table. Price them as separate lines, like a contractor would. A client who says no to a $35 oven clean today often says yes in month three, because the line is already on the sheet.

## What moves a cleaning price up or down?

Up: first visits, deep cleans, move out work, large homes, many bathrooms, pet hair, heavy soap scum or grease, long travel, and one time jobs with no repeat booked. A one time job has the same drive and setup as a repeat job and no future visits to spread it over, so it should cost more per visit.

Down: weekly service, small homes near other clients on the same route, and homes the client keeps tidy between visits. Weekly homes can run 20 to 30 percent below a one time standard price and still pay well, because the time per visit drops the most.

Avoid per room pricing as your main method. HomeGuide lists $30 to $50 per room, but a small bedroom and a greasy kitchen are not equal work. Use it only for a rough phone quote. Flat per visit pricing suits repeat clients and rewards speed. Hourly pricing protects you on first visits.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much should I charge for a 2,000 sq ft house?
For a standard clean, HomeGuide range for 2,000 sq ft is $190 to $340 for regular cleaning, with many quotes near $200. Deep cleaning for that size runs $300 to $600 on the same source. Your time estimate decides where in the range you land.

### Is it better to charge by the hour or a flat rate?
Flat rate for repeat clients, hourly protection for first and deep cleans. Flat rates are easier for clients to accept and pay you more as you get faster. Hourly is safer when you cannot judge the condition of a home in advance.

### How much extra is a deep clean over a standard clean?
Plan on 1.5 to 2 times the standard price. In the worked example, a $200 standard clean became a $360 deep clean for the same home. The extra time goes to baseboards, appliances, tracks, and detail work a standard visit skips.

### What discount should I give for weekly or biweekly cleaning?
A 10 to 20 percent cut from the one time price is common, and it should reflect real time saved, not just a sales offer. If a biweekly home takes 3 hours against 4 hours for a one time visit, the time saving alone supports the discount.

### Should I charge more for pet homes?
Yes, if pets add time. Pet hair on furniture and stairs can add 30 to 60 minutes to a visit. Name the charge in the quote as extra time at your hourly rate, so the client sees the reason, not a penalty.

### Do I need insurance to charge pro rates?
Yes, if you want company level rates. Clients paying $50 to $75 per hour expect a bonded and insured business that sends a replacement if you are sick. Solo cleaners without cover usually sit at the low end of the range.

## Next step
